At the end of each round, players score points as a measurement of their progress. In a four-player game, the game ends after the 7th round. The winner is the player with the most points. On your turn, you must either resolve an action or pass. To resolve an action, choose an unoccupied action space and place as many workers as required on that space. Then, resolve that action. ! Action spaces on the game board (and any engineers on it) let you resolve direct actions. All other actions, if not specifically labeled as direct, are indirect actions. ! Note: You cannot save actions for your next turn. Playing a turn Each turn a player will choose an empty/unoccupied action space, occupy it with the required number of workers and perform that action. You must consider the following: You must choose an unoccupied action space (i.e. one that is not already occupied by workers). You must place the exact/correct number of workers from your supply on the required action space you wish to use (i.e. 1, 2 or 3). You must only use workers from your personal worker supply. You must immediately make use of the direct/chosen action or pass. You must perform the direct action in its entirety. Engineers you have hired count as indirect actions. You can partially resolve these actions. You may perform only one action per turn. Actions that become available to you (either by choosing an action space or otherwise) during your turn go into your action pool. This means that you can resolve these actions during your turn, in any order you choose. You can also choose not to resolve indirect actions. Note: Exceptions to these rules will be noted where applicable. The areas of the board (possible actions) 1. Track extension 2. Locomotives and factories 3. Industrialization 4. Auxiliary actions 5. Engineers 6. Turn order track 1. TRACK EXTENSION The track extension actions are among the most important in the game. Each player’s personal player board depicts 3 railroads, which can be independently extended over the course of the game. These railroads are called Trans-Siberian railroad, Petersburg railroad and the Kiev railroad. The better each of their railroads is developed, the more points each player will score at the end of each round. First, place the required number of workers on one of the track extension action spaces. Then, advance the appropriate track(s) on your player board the number of spaces indicated on the action space. You may choose to distribute track advancements between multiple railroads. And so ends the action. In order to earn more points, the players should strive to extend their railroads through the advancement of these tracks. To maximize their progress, players will also need to advance tracks of other colors, indicating tracks of higher value. In order to advance the tracks in the other colors, you must first earn them. [Rating: 2/10] Unbelievably dry and frankly completely uninteresting to me.  It's the type of game I've come to dislike extremely much in the genre. Expansions in general merely serve to add more and more convoluted mechanisms at every higher prices.  I've been intrigued by Russian Railroads for years and found it so underwhelming it was an instant salad.  There are games that do everything this does better.

[Rating: 3/10] One of the best games in my collection is the Russian Railroads board game with its expansions. But this version is very terrible. I don't undestand why they mixed the colors and the signs in this version. It was the most wanted game for me in this year, but now I think, i do not buy it. I'm very happy, because i did not sell the original game.

[Rating: 3/10] I played this on BGA and did not find it to be a railroad game, or ultimate. To me this is an abstract worker placement game with a railroad theme tacked on. The point scoring is overly complex, and I would never want to try this game outside of BGA where points are taken care of automatically.  I also found the layout of the board and iconography very frustrating to learn, with NOTHING being intuitive. [Rating: 4/10] Lay tracks, score points, lay tracks, score points, lay tracks, score points. If Russian Railroads tries to convey the monotonous feeling of building a railroad, they are very successful. If it tries to provide a fun gaming experience, I see no need to play more than one round.  Granted, there is room for interaction where you try to find (literal) tracks that will meet as little competition as possible to optimize each and every action but surely a game should offer more than that.  Ultimate Railroads offer some more options but the gameplay remains monotonous.

[Rating: 4/10] EFORP9 - Not my first play but apparently I never logged it. Played Russian Railroads the first time and American Railroads this time. I'm sure this is a good game and all but just not for me. Don't find the gameplay particularly interesting and also I'm super bad at it. Not really fun enough for me to want to play it more to get better.

[Rating: 5/10] Tried the Asian track variant and it seemed overly fiddly and not that appealing.

[Rating: 5/10] I get why ppl like this, but I just don't.  I like dry and mechanical but this game just shows its gears to blatantly for me to really get invested.   You are basically building your own multiplication on different tracks and has none of the obfuscation of how to win which e.g. makes Uwe Rosenberg games so good and repayable.  It feels like the perfect game for AI figure out.

[Rating: 5/10] Played the base board on BGA and they have changed a few things but nothing significant. Overall this won't change my opinion of the game that is just a whole bunch of math and moving along tracks. I can tolerate this on BGA where all the math is done for me, and I can just focus on my turns and not all the counting each round. I'll be happy to play this on BGA on occasion with a few gaming friends, but never one I'd suggest myself.
